## What You Will Produce

- An original **two-part content analysis**
    - A qualitative phase that builds coding variables through immersion
    - A quantitative phase that tests relationships
- A **Research Proposal** written as a structured sentence outline

- Work at a level approaching publishable quality

## Two Words From That List

::: {.define}
**Content analysis:** the systematic study of messages; in its quantitative form, the one this course uses, you sort each message into categories by written rules so the results can be counted. Example: marking each chat message as aimed at the streamer, at another viewer, or at the whole room, then counting each kind.
:::

::: {.define}
**Immersion:** spending sustained time with your material, watching and reading it closely, before you analyze it. Example: hours of one channel's streams and chat before you write a single category.
:::

## Two Words for What You Build

::: {.define}
**Variable:** something about a case that can change from one case to the next, where a case is one thing you study, such as one chat message. Example: the `game` column says Fortnite for one stream and Just Chatting for another.
:::

::: {.define}
**Codebook:** the written rules that tell a coder what each variable means and which value to give each item; in this course the word also covers the coding sheet where you record those values. Example: the rule that a message tagging the streamer is coded "directed at the streamer."
:::

## Who Makes That Determination

::: {.define}
**Institutional Review Board (IRB):** the committee that oversees research involving people, reviewing each study before it starts to protect the people in it. Example: SIUE's IRB decides whether a study of public chat counts as human subjects research.
:::

## The Shared Example Dataset

[One week of Twitch, November 2018]{.eyebrow}

- **21,964,296 chat messages** across 1,695 channels
- **590,876 stream snapshots**: who streamed what, to how many people
- The data is public, messy, and real, collected by an automated process across six days
- It plays three roles you must not conflate, and which role a claim rests on determines what the claim can say
    - The **population**: 1,690 channels in both logs
    - The **working corpus**: 50 channels, stratified by chat volume
    - The **anchor set**: 8 channels used as named examples
- This dataset is the shared example for the class. Your own study uses the source your question needs

## Two Words for the Example Data

::: {.define}
**Snapshot:** one record of one stream at one moment, taken about once a minute: its channel, title, game, viewer count, and time. Example: xQc streaming Just Chatting to 19,381 viewers at one moment on November 18, 2018.
:::

::: {.define}
**Population:** everything your conclusions will apply to, defined by the platform, the accounts or outlets, and the time period. Example: the 1,690 channels in both logs, that November week.
:::

## Two More Words for the Example Data

::: {.define}
**Corpus:** a collection of texts or records gathered to be studied as a set. Example: the working corpus, the chat and snapshots of 50 channels.
:::

::: {.define}
**Stratified sampling:** split the population into groups, called **strata** (one group is a **stratum**), then draw from each group separately. Example: the working corpus draws channels from every chat-volume group.
:::

## The Four Tools

::: {.define}
**R:** a free language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. Example: R counts how many messages each channel posted that week.
:::

::: {.define}
**VS Code:** a free code editor from Microsoft, where you write code and prose in one place. Example: your White Paper's text and its R code open side by side in one window.
:::

- All four are free, and setup walkthroughs are on the course site

## The Four Tools, Continued

::: {.define}
**Quarto:** an open-source publishing system that turns one file of text and code into a finished website, PDF, or paper. Example: your White Paper is a single Quarto file.
:::

::: {.define}
**Git:** a program that tracks every change to the files in a project, so you can see or return to any earlier version. **GitHub:** a website that hosts those Git projects online. Example: your project's full history sits on GitHub, one dated change at a time.
:::

- Your White Paper and your poster will both be built from Quarto sources
- Version control is not a convenience here. It is your audit trail

## What R Looks Like

A full analysis, start to finish:

```r
library(v2v)
chat <- twitch_chat()

chat %>%
  group_by(channel) %>%
  summarize(messages = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(messages))
```

Read it as: take the chat data, group it by channel, count the messages, and sort from most
to least. Code is instructions in order, and you will read far more of it than you write.

## Two Numbers From One Week on Twitch

[Chapter 1]{.eyebrow}

- **Bob Ross:** 3,178 average viewers, streaming under *Art*, and dead since 1995
- **xQc:** 17,363 average viewers, live variety, and the highest chat volume in the collection
- A social scientist asks not what the numbers *mean* but what they *are*

::: {.define}
**Data:** observations recorded on purpose, as numbers or as labels, so a claim can be checked later. Example: Bob Ross's 3,178 average viewers is a number; his category, *Art*, is a label.
:::

- A corpus can answer some questions and not others

## Stories and Science Share One Machinery

- **Barrett:** the brain is a **prediction machine** that updates its models on error
- **Storr:** **stories** are cognitive tools for simulating cause and effect
- Science is the same narrative machinery under **rigor** and a public record
- Babbie's everyday ways of knowing are tradition, authority, common sense, and intuition
    - Each serves daily life, and each breaks when others must trust the result

## The Sacred Flaw and the Null Hypothesis

::: {.define}
**Null hypothesis:** the claim that there is no real difference or relationship, only chance. Example: gaming and non-gaming streams draw the same average audience.
:::

- The null is research's sacred flaw: it says *nothing is happening here*, and to reject it is to force the data to tell a different story than you assumed
- The framing puts the burden where it belongs: on the evidence, not on the elegance of your argument

## Reading a *p*-Value

::: {.define}
**p-value:** how likely a gap at least this big would be if the null hypothesis were true. Below .05 is called *statistically significant*.
:::

- A *p* of 0.001 says the old story is untenable, not merely unlikely

## The Debt Cliff That Was Not There

[Reinhart and Rogoff, 2010]{.eyebrow}

- Their finding said public debt above 90% of GDP crushes growth, and it shaped austerity policy
- In 2013 a doctoral student replicating it for a class could not match the numbers
- The original spreadsheet held an Excel error that excluded several countries
- Corrected, growth above the threshold was **+2.2%**, not −0.1%
- The error was caught because the work was **transparent enough to retrace**, which is the mechanism working, not failing

## Discussion: A Manifesto for Reproducible Science {.discuss}

On Munafò et al. (2017), "A manifesto for reproducible science," answer each in writing:

- The paper names four threats: low power, analytic flexibility, publication bias, and poor reporting. Name the one that most endangers a content analysis study like the ones we are building, and give one reason
- The authors argue the fixes must change **incentives**, not just habits. State whether you accept that, and why
- State whether pre-registration is always appropriate, or name one kind of question it constrains unfairly
- Write down one sentence from the paper you would quote in your own methods section

## What Makes a Scholarly Contribution

A contribution in communication research does one of four things:

1. **Tests a theory** in a new context
2. **Replicates a finding** with new data
3. **Resolves a conflict** between findings in the literature
4. **Introduces a testable construct**

Before you design a study, name which one you are doing. If you cannot say precisely, the
research question is not ready yet.

## What a Construct Is

::: {.define}
**Construct:** an abstract idea that a theory uses to explain something, and that a study has to find a way to measure. Example: parasocial attachment, a viewer's one-sided sense of closeness to a streamer, which you can only measure through what viewers write.
:::

## The Reproducibility Crisis Is a Design Problem

::: {.define}
**Garden of forking paths:** the many defensible choices made during an analysis, each of which could have gone another way, which together raise the chance of a false positive with no conscious fishing at all (Gelman & Loken, 2014). Example: deciding after seeing the data whether to drop bot messages.
:::

- Munafò and colleagues locate a related danger in underpowered designs:

> "Low statistical power increases the likelihood of obtaining both false-positive and false-negative results, meaning that it offers no advantage if the purpose is to accumulate knowledge."
>
> Munafò et al. (2017, p. 2)

## Three Terms Behind That Quote

::: {.define}
**False positive:** concluding that an effect exists when it does not, by rejecting a null hypothesis that is true. Example: reporting that gaming chat is louder when the gap came from chance alone.
:::

::: {.define}
**Statistical power:** the chance your study detects an effect that is really there. Example: with only 80 messages, a real but small gap between gaming and non-gaming chat could easily go unseen.
:::

::: {.define}
**Underpowered:** a sample too small to give the study a good chance of detecting the effect it looks for. Example: 80 messages, when a small effect would take far more to detect.
:::

## Four Pillars This Course Builds

- **A priori power:** committing to a sample size before collection
- **Pre-registration:** committing to hypotheses, measures, and an analysis plan first
- **Coding reliability:** re-coding a subsample after a gap to show the codebook holds regardless of when it is applied
- **An audit trail:** a version-controlled record from raw data to published figure

These are not add-ons. They follow from the epistemology you are adopting.

## Two Pillars, Defined

::: {.define}
**A priori power analysis:** working out, before you collect data, how large a sample you need to detect an effect of a given size. Example: deciding how many messages to code before drawing any.
:::

::: {.define}
**Pre-registration:** writing down your research plan, including hypotheses, measures, and analysis, and filing it with a registry before you study the data. Example: a dated plan stating which test you will run on which variables.
:::

## Pre-Registration, Precisely

> "The strongest form of pre-registration involves both registering the study ... and closely pre-specifying the study design, primary outcome and analysis plan in advance of conducting the study or knowing the outcomes of the research."
>
> Munafò et al. (2017, p. 3)

- Pre-registration is what separates **confirmatory** from **exploratory** work
- Exploratory research is legitimate. Presenting it as confirmatory is not

## Confirmatory and Exploratory

::: {.define}
**Confirmatory research:** testing a prediction you made before seeing the data. Example: a pre-registered test of whether non-gaming chats address the streamer more often.
:::

::: {.define}
**Exploratory research:** looking through data for patterns you did not predict, to generate ideas for later tests. Example: browsing the chat table to see which kinds of messages cluster around raids.
:::

## A Study Is a Story Told With Discipline

| In a story | In a study |
|---|---|
| Inciting incident | The research problem, an anomaly |
| Protagonist | The researcher as detective |
| Antagonist | Confounds, sampling bias, measurement error |
| Rising action | Literature review and theory |
| Climax | The statistical test |
| Falling action | Interpretation and limitations |
| Resolution | Implications and future research |

## Three Words From That Table

::: {.define}
**Literature review:** a written overview of what published research has already found on a topic, and how those studies fit together. Example: summarizing the published studies of Twitch chat before you design your own.
:::

::: {.define}
**Theory:** a set of connected ideas that explains and predicts why something happens, within stated limits. Example: parasocial interaction explains why viewers talk to a streamer as if they knew them.
:::

::: {.define}
**Sampling bias:** a way of drawing a sample in which some members of the population are more likely to be picked than others. Example: studying only the biggest channels.
:::

## Anecdote and Data Are Partners

- **Journalism** makes the abstract concrete and makes an audience care
- **Science** establishes generalizability: it asks whether the pattern holds across many cases
- Anecdotes generate hypotheses, and data test them. Data find patterns, and anecdotes explain why they matter

## Hypotheses and Human Context

::: {.define}
**Hypothesis:** a testable statement of the relationship you expect between variables, written before you test it. Example: non-gaming chats aim a larger share of their messages at the streamer than gaming chats do.
:::

- A significant finding without human context is true and unpersuasive
- Your White Paper has to carry both the pattern and the people, which is harder than it sounds

## Three Paradigms

- We work in a **social scientific** paradigm: hypotheses tested against data
- **Interpretive** work asks how people make meaning, through interviews and ethnography
- **Critical** work exposes and challenges structures of power
- All three have produced foundational communication scholarship

## Placing Your Own Question

::: {.define}
**Paradigm:** a shared set of beliefs about what reality is and how researchers can know it, which shapes how a study is designed. Example: the social scientific paradigm treats chat as something you can observe and count.
:::

- Place your own research question on the axis from ontology (what exists) to epistemology (how we can know it), and name one obligation that follows from that placement
